AI for Mobility · Vision backbones · ViT to Swin

What a 224-pixel square cannot see, and how Swin pays for the rest

A Vision Transformer reads a 224×224 square. A forward camera on a Florida street delivers 1928×1208. This page measures what happens in between, on a real clip of a child on a kick scooter: where ViT loses the child, what it costs to keep every pixel, and how Swin's three moves (windows, shifted windows, merging) fix both problems. It ends with the cameras where Swin is the right call and the ones where it is not.

Three ways to hand a camera frame to a ViT

An ADAS perception stack has to find the child on the scooter early, while there is still time to brake. A ViT trained on ImageNet expects a 224×224 square, so something has to happen to the 1928×1208 frame first. Pick a way to feed it and watch what reaches the model.

Why ViT wants the square. Besides its weights, a ViT learns one position vector for each of its 14×14 = 196 patch slots, plus one for the class token. Run it on a bigger frame and the position table has to be stretched. ViT-Tiny's table went from rows at 224×224 to at 1088×1920, taking the parameter count from to . The new rows are interpolated, never trained.

Keep the pixels, and every token pays for every other token

Option three keeps the child. The price is in how attention works: each token compares itself with every other token, in every head of every layer. Double the frame's width and height and the token count goes up 4×, but the pairs go up 16×.

Camera

ViT-S/16: 384 numbers per token, 6 heads, 12 layers. Frames are padded to whole 16-px patches. One extra class token is counted in the pairs. Multiply-accumulates (MACs) for the backbone only, counted with PyTorch's FLOP counter, attention included.

The one equation (Swin paper, eq. 1)

Ω(MSA) = 4·hw·C² + 2·(hw)²·C h × w token grid (76 × 121 on the forward camera) C numbers per token first term project every token to query, key, value, output: grows with tokens second term compare every token with every token: grows with tokens SQUARED

In words: the first term is paid once per token, the second once per pair. On a 224 square the pairs are a footnote, of ViT-S's work. On a 1080p intersection camera they are , and on 4K drone video .

Going deeper: memory-efficient attention changes the memory, not the arithmetic

The table above lists the attention matrix in gigabytes “if stored”. Modern kernels (FlashAttention and PyTorch's fused CPU kernel) never store the full matrix; they stream through it in blocks. That removes the memory wall but not the multiply-adds: every pair is still computed. It is also why the counts here were taken with attention written as plain matrix products. With the fused kernel switched on, the FLOP counter skipped attention entirely and reported ViT-S at 224 as 4.24 G instead of 4.60 G. The timing runs did use the fused kernel, so the measured seconds are what an efficient implementation actually costs.

Read the left end of the chart honestly. At FL511's 720×480, plain ViT-S took s and Swin-T s on the same CPU. ViT-S was faster. Below about one megapixel the pair term is not yet the bill, and window bookkeeping has overhead. The cost argument for Swin is an argument about high-resolution cameras and drones.

One grid for a child who grows 7.65× in 5.55 seconds

A detector reads objects off feature maps. ViT offers one map at stride 16 in every layer. A CNN or Swin offers four: strides 4, 8, 16 and 32. Pick a backbone and a map and see how many cells the child covers when it first appears and when it is closest.

Backbone
Feature map

Boxes are the detector's boxes on the native frame (frames 78 and 188), drawn to scale on a neutral background. Each square is one cell of the chosen map.

What the pyramid buys. A small, distant object needs a fine map, or it collapses into one or two cells that also contain kerb and trees. A large, near object needs a coarse map, or it spreads over dozens or hundreds of cells, and no 3×3 kernel or 7×7 window sees all of it at once. A detector with a feature pyramid (FPN) reads small boxes from fine levels and large boxes from coarse ones. With a single stride-16 map, both cases have to be read from the same grid.
The experiment that settles it. To put a plain ViT (DeiT-S) into their detection benchmark, the Swin authors had to bolt deconvolution layers onto it to manufacture a pyramid. Even then it trailed Swin-T while costing more (tab 5).

Swin: attention in windows, windows that shift, tokens that merge

Swin keeps attention's content-dependent weights and gives back two things the CNN had: locality and a pyramid. Step through Swin-T's 12 blocks on the forward camera and watch two things: the window the token attends inside (gold), and everything that can influence that token so far (dashed). Then switch to ViT-S and ResNet-50 for comparison. Click the frame to follow a different token.

Backbone
Block
 
this block's window (Swin) or kernel (ResNet) can influence the token so far the token you follow

The three moves

  • Windows. Cut the token grid into 7×7 windows. Attention runs inside each window only: 49 comparisons per token instead of all of them.
  • Shifted windows. Every second block, move the window grid by ⌊7/2⌋ = 3 tokens. Tokens near a border now share a window with their neighbours across it.
  • Merging. Between stages, fuse each 2×2 block of tokens into one: 4× fewer tokens, 2× more channels. Strides 4, 8, 16, 32, the same as ResNet-50's four stages.

The cost, rewritten (Swin paper, eq. 2)

Ω(W-MSA) = 4·hw·C² + 2·M²·hw·C M = 7, the window side. The pair term now grows with hw, not (hw)².

On the forward camera at stride 16: ViT-S compares pairs per head per layer, Swin , fewer.

A transportation way to hold it. A county signal system run as coordination zones: controllers coordinate within their zone, never with every controller in the county. Shifted windows are redrawing the zone boundaries every other cycle, so a platoon that crossed a boundary is inside one zone next time. Merging is going from intersection-level to corridor-level control.
Going deeper: the edge mask, relative positions, and why these regions are upper bounds
  • Shifting without extra windows. Swin rolls the feature map 3 tokens up and to the left, partitions it as usual, and masks attention between tokens that were not neighbours before the roll, then rolls it back. The window count stays the same as the regular block.
  • Relative position bias. Inside a window Swin adds a learned bias to every attention logit, softmax(QKᵀ/√d + B)V. The bias depends only on the offset between the two tokens, (2M−1)² = 169 possible offsets per head. Nothing is tied to an absolute slot, so a bigger camera needs no stretched position table.
  • Theoretical vs effective receptive field. The dashed region is everything that can influence the token. In trained networks the influence concentrates near the centre and fades quickly (Luo et al., NeurIPS 2016). Read the region as an upper bound, for all three backbones.

Does Swin detect better? The benchmark, and the catch

The mechanism says Swin should help. The benchmark checks whether it does. Here is the comparison the Swin authors ran, the CNN that answered it a year later, and the cost of each backbone measured on this page's cameras.

COCO detection, Cascade Mask R-CNN, 3× schedule (Swin paper, Table 2b)

† DeiT-S is a plain ViT. The authors added deconvolution layers so it could hand the detector a feature pyramid. FPS as reported in the paper.

The catch: a modern CNN ties it (ConvNeXt paper, Table 3)

ConvNeXt-T is a ResNet rebuilt with Swin's design and training choices: larger kernels, fewer activations, the same four-stage pyramid. It matches Swin-T on detection and runs faster. The lesson is not “transformers beat CNNs”. It is that locality, a pyramid and a modern training recipe win, whether the blocks are attention or convolution.

Why ViT needs more data: the ViT paper in its own words

“” and so, “”

Trained on ImageNet-1k only, Swin-T reaches % top-1 at GFLOPs, DeiT-S % at , and ViT-B/16 at 384×384 % at (Swin paper, Table 1a). Locality is cheap prior knowledge, and Swin gets it back.

Before you trust this result. Baseline: ResNet-50 at matched compute, which is a fair one. Split: COCO validation images, everyday photos, not Florida roads. Ugly cases: night, rain, glare, and a pedestrian who is six pixels tall are not what this number measures. Re-run the comparison on your own footage, with whole cameras held out of training.

Fit card: Swin

Idea in one sentence
Attention inside small shifting windows, merged into a four-level pyramid.
Why it works (the logic)
Weights computed from the content, like ViT; locality and four scales, like a CNN; cost that grows with pixels instead of pixels squared.
Fits these tasks
Boxes or masks on full-resolution camera frames: vulnerable road users, turning-movement counts, lane and pavement maps (extraction, classification).
Needs this data
ImageNet-pretrained weights, plus hundreds to thousands of box- or pixel-labelled frames from your own cameras, split by camera.
Breaks when
Latency or power is tight on a roadside or in-vehicle box; objects are only a few pixels even at stride 4; you train from scratch on a small dataset.
Keep the classical method when
You need one label per frame (a plain ViT or CNN at 224 is enough), the edge accelerator is built around convolution, or you only need volumes (loops and radar already count).

Check yourself

  1. A county wants 15-minute turning-movement counts from 40 existing 1080p intersection cameras, computed on a box in each signal cabinet. ViT-S, Swin-T or ResNet-50? What would you measure before deciding?
    One way to answer

    Not ViT-S: at 1080p it needs × Swin-T's multiply-adds. Between Swin-T and ResNet-50, measure latency on the cabinet hardware itself and accuracy on that county's night and rain footage, with whole cameras held out of training. The 4-point COCO gap is a reason to test Swin, not a reason to skip the test.

  2. A colleague proposes replacing Lab 6's ViT-Tiny with Swin-T “because Swin is better.” For one congestion label per 720×480 FL511 frame, what does it buy and what does it cost?
    One way to answer

    One label per frame needs no pyramid and no small-object detail, so nothing obvious. At 224×224 Swin-T costs GMAC against ViT-Tiny's , about × more, and at 720×480 it was slower than ViT-S on this CPU. If the label is wrong after dark, the teacher is the problem (Lab 6), not the backbone.

  3. A drone vendor offers 4K top-down video of an interchange, and the team plans to run ViT-S on every full frame. What breaks first, and what would you use instead?
    One way to answer

    The pair count: tokens, TMAC per frame, GB per layer if the attention matrix were stored. Shrinking to 224 turns a car into px. From straight above every car is the same size, so a CNN segmenter is enough. That is how highD was built.
